hero.headline: US strikes Iran for second time this week despite ceasefire
hero.body:
The United States conducted new strikes on military targets in southern Iran on Wednesday, marking the second attack in three days while a ceasefire between the two countries remains officially in place. Both nations are simultaneously engaged in peace negotiations aimed at ending the three-month conflict.

A US official confirmed the strikes targeted attack drones and a drone ground control station, describing the military action as a self-defense measure. The attacks occurred near the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway critical to global energy supplies that handles roughly one-fifth of the world's oil transport.

Oil prices rose immediately following news of the strikes. The Trump administration has denied reaching any agreement with Iran regarding passage through the strategic waterway.

The fresh military action threatens the fragile ceasefire that both countries have maintained during diplomatic talks. The strikes represent a pattern of continued US military operations that risk undermining peace efforts, even as negotiators from both sides work toward a comprehensive agreement.

The military site targeted in the strikes underscores their strategic importance. The narrow Strait of Hormuz serves as a chokepoint for global energy supplies, making the region's security a matter of international concern beyond US-Iran relations alone.

Iran had imposed a near-total internet shutdown lasting 88 days during the conflict. The government recently began allowing citizens to reconnect with the outside world, though access remains limited and uncertain. Many Iranians remain unsure how long the restored connectivity will persist.

The pattern of military strikes followed by continued diplomatic negotiations illustrates the unstable nature of the current ceasefire. While military commanders conduct operations they view as necessary for national security, diplomatic teams continue working toward a permanent resolution.

Neither the US government nor Iran has publicly stated how the latest strikes will affect ongoing peace talks. The renewed military action raises significant questions about whether the ceasefire can remain stable long enough for negotiators to reach an agreement that would end the war.

The strikes come after a three-month period of conflict between the two countries. Previous US military operations occurred just days earlier, making Wednesday's attack the latest in a series of operations that complicate diplomatic efforts. Both governments have characterized the ceasefire as fragile, acknowledging the difficulty of maintaining peace while military operations continue.

The timing and location of these strikes demonstrate how security concerns continue to drive military decisions even as political leaders pursue negotiations. The international community, particularly nations dependent on Middle Eastern oil supplies, watches closely as the situation develops.

cards.headline: Justice Department opens criminal investigation into Trump accuser E. Jean Carroll
cards.body:
The Department of Justice has opened a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, who accused President Trump of sexual assault, according to multiple reports.

CNN first reported the investigation on Wednesday night. The probe focuses on whether Carroll committed perjury while speaking at a deposition as part of her two civil lawsuits against Trump.

Carroll sued Trump twice in civil court. The first lawsuit alleged defamation after Trump denied her allegations of sexual assault. A second lawsuit made similar claims. Both cases resulted in verdicts against Trump, with juries awarding Carroll substantial damages.

The investigation represents a significant shift in the legal battles between Trump and Carroll. Previously, Trump faced civil liability in courts over his denials of Carroll's allegations. The criminal probe now places Carroll herself under scrutiny by federal prosecutors.

Perjury charges require prosecutors to prove that a witness knowingly made false statements under oath during official proceedings. Depositions in civil lawsuits carry the same legal weight as courtroom testimony, and witnesses face potential criminal penalties for lying.

The Justice Department has not publicly commented on the investigation. Federal prosecutors in criminal cases typically decline to confirm or deny ongoing investigations until charges are filed.

Carroll's attorneys have not issued public statements about the probe. The investigation's scope and timeline remain unknown.

The development adds another layer to the years-long legal conflict between Trump and Carroll. Her initial allegations dated back decades but became public when she published a memoir detailing the alleged assault. Trump's denials led to the defamation lawsuits that ultimately resulted in the depositions now under investigation.

The criminal investigation proceeds separately from the civil cases, which have concluded with judgments against Trump. Federal investigators will examine deposition transcripts and other evidence to determine whether Carroll's statements meet the legal threshold for perjury charges.

cards.headline: U.S. military shoots down Iranian drones, strikes launch site in Strait of Hormuz
cards.teaser: The U.S. military shot down four Iranian attack drones and struck a ground control station preparing to launch a fifth drone.
cards.body:
The U.S. military intercepted four Iranian attack drones in the Strait of Hormuz and struck a ground control station in Bandar Abbas that was preparing to launch a fifth drone. Iran's military had directed the drones at a commercial ship in the strait.

This confrontation represents the second such clash within 48 hours. The incident comes as the U.S. and Iran continue negotiating to resolve their conflict. President Trump's recent statements indicate he is maintaining strict demands in the negotiations.

cards.headline: Israel orders evacuations across southern Lebanon as fighting intensifies
cards.teaser: The Israeli military declared areas south of the Zahrani River to be combat zones and warned of fresh strikes against Hezbollah.
cards.body:
The Israeli military has ordered residents to evacuate large areas of southern Lebanon south of the Zahrani River, designating these regions as active combat zones. The evacuation directive comes as the military threatens fresh strikes against Hezbollah targets in the area.

The escalating orders and military threats represent a significant intensification of hostilities between Israel and the Lebanese militant group, even as diplomatic efforts continue to address the broader regional conflict.

cards.headline: FBI arrests former CIA officer with $40 million in gold bars at home
cards.teaser: Prosecutors say a former CIA official stole 300 gold bars from the agency.
cards.body:
Federal authorities arrested David Rush, a former CIA officer, after discovering approximately $40 million worth of gold bars at his home. Prosecutors allege Rush stole 300 gold bars from the agency.

The FBI executed the arrest following an investigation into the missing gold. According to charging documents, Rush allegedly defrauded the government by lying about his credentials. Sources familiar with the case confirmed the substantial quantity of gold recovered from his residence.

cards.headline: Paper mill disaster in Longview may be deadliest industrial tragedy in modern Washington history
cards.teaser: Two people are confirmed dead and nine remain missing after a chemical vat implosion at a Longview facility.
cards.body:
A chemical tank ruptured at Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co in Longview on Tuesday morning, killing two workers and leaving nine others missing and presumed dead. One person died after being hospitalized following the disaster.

Washington's governor called it a potential deadliest industrial tragedy in modern state history. The incident involved white liquor, a caustic chemical used in paper manufacturing. Contaminated water from the rupture flowed through Longview's drainage system as authorities managed the environmental fallout.

cards.headline: Google engineer charged with insider trading after $1.2 million profit on Polymarket
cards.body:
Federal authorities have charged a Google engineer with insider trading after the individual made $1.2 million through bets placed on the prediction market platform Polymarket.

According to the criminal complaint, the engineer wagered over $2.7 million on bets related to Google's 2025 Year in Search campaign. The charges suggest the engineer used confidential information obtained through their position at the technology company to place the wagers.

Polymarket is a prediction market platform where users can bet on the outcomes of future events, ranging from political elections to corporate announcements. The platform has grown in popularity as an alternative way to forecast events through market-based predictions.

The case marks a notable intersection between traditional insider trading enforcement and newer prediction market platforms. While insider trading prosecutions typically involve traditional stock markets, this case demonstrates that authorities are applying the same legal framework to trading on prediction markets when nonpublic information is involved.

The complaint indicates the engineer risked a substantial sum on wagers tied specifically to outcomes related to Google's annual Year in Search campaign, which highlights trending searches and cultural moments from the year. The timing and specificity of the bets apparently drew the attention of investigators.

The $1.2 million profit represents the gains allegedly made from the trades, while the $2.7 million figure reflects the total amount wagered across the related bets. The engineer would have had access to internal Google information about the campaign before it became public.

Federal insider trading laws prohibit trading securities or other instruments based on material nonpublic information. Prosecutors have increasingly applied these statutes beyond traditional stock trading to encompass various financial instruments and markets.

The case is part of ongoing efforts by financial regulators and law enforcement to monitor activity on prediction markets, which have operated in a regulatory gray area. As these platforms have gained users and trading volume, they have attracted greater scrutiny from authorities concerned about potential market manipulation and the misuse of confidential information.

cards.headline: Former federal judges ask court to investigate Trump IRS settlement
cards.teaser: A bipartisan group of former federal judges requested a court reopen Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over a settlement creating a $1.776 billion fund.
cards.body:
A bipartisan group of former federal judges has asked a federal court to reopen President Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. They argue the administration bypassed normal judicial oversight by negotiating a settlement directly with the president.

The settlement established a $1.776 billion fund intended to compensate alleged "victims of lawfare and weaponization." The judges question whether proper legal procedures were followed in reaching the agreement, seeking court investigation into how the settlement was structured and executed.

cards.headline: Australia files $2 billion lawsuit against 3M over contaminated defense sites
cards.teaser: The government is suing the US manufacturer over chemicals in firefighting foam that contaminated military installations.
cards.body:
The Australian government has launched its largest legal claim ever, seeking more than A$2 billion in damages from multinational manufacturer 3M. The lawsuit addresses contamination at defense bases caused by per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) used in firefighting foam.

Known as "forever chemicals," PFAS persist indefinitely in the environment and the human body. Attorney General Michelle Rowland announced the legal action against 3M over the chemical contamination at Australian military installations.

cards.headline: Pakistan and Afghanistan continue fighting months after war declaration
cards.teaser: Neither side appears ready to back down despite mediation efforts by China.
cards.body:
Pakistan declared "open war" on Afghanistan months ago, and neither side has shown signs of backing down. The conflict remains active with no immediate resolution in sight.

China has attempted to mediate between the two countries but has not succeeded in brokering peace. The dispute reflects long-standing tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan that have proven resistant to diplomatic intervention.

cards.headline: Pork prices in China fall to 16-year low
cards.teaser: The drop signals weak consumer spending and oversupply in the country's hog market.
cards.body:
China's pork prices have dropped to their lowest point in 16 years, reflecting significant economic headwinds. The collapse is driven by weak consumer spending and an oversupply of hogs flooding the market faster than buyers can absorb them.

Pork serves as a critical inflation gauge in China given its central role in the national diet. The sharp price decline underscores mounting pressure on household finances and the broader challenge of excess production in the sector.

cards.headline: California court rejects Tesla bid to dismiss racial discrimination lawsuit
cards.teaser: A court ruling allows the state civil rights agency to proceed with its case against the automaker, with trial set for July.
cards.body:
A California court has rejected Tesla's motion to dismiss a racial discrimination lawsuit filed by the state's civil rights agency. The ruling allows the case to move forward to trial.

The civil rights agency expressed satisfaction with the court's decision and indicated the case is expected to go to trial in July. The lawsuit alleges racial discrimination at Tesla.

cards.headline: Georgia coach suggests SEC could leave NCAA without playoff agreement
cards.teaser: Kirby Smart raised the possibility of the SEC essentially seceding from the NCAA if conference expansion talks do not reach a resolution.
cards.body:
Georgia head coach Kirby Smart suggested Tuesday that the SEC could leave the NCAA if negotiations fail to produce an agreement on playoff expansion and related issues. His remarks came during college football's spring meetings, where conference expansion has been a dominant topic of discussion.

Smart's comments represent one of the most forceful statements yet about how far conferences might go to protect their interests as ongoing negotiations continue.

cards.headline: Hurricanes take 3-1 series lead with shutout over Canadiens
cards.teaser: Frederik Andersen stopped 18 shots in his third playoff shutout this postseason as Carolina moved within one win of the Stanley Cup Final.
cards.body:
Frederik Andersen made 18 saves to shut out the Canadiens and give the Hurricanes a 3-1 series lead in the Eastern Conference finals. The victory puts Carolina one win away from advancing to the Stanley Cup Final.

Andersen has now recorded three shutouts in 12 playoff games this postseason. His performance helped the Hurricanes take command of the series as they seek their first trip to the Final in several years.

cards.headline: Appeals court allows pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil to remain free pending Supreme Court petition
cards.teaser: A federal appeals panel let activist Mahmoud Khalil stay free while he takes his case against the Trump administration to the Supreme Court.
cards.body:
Original Card Text

A three-judge panel of the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals allowed pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil to remain free as he petitions the Supreme Court. Judges Stephanos Bibas, Arianna Freeman and Thomas Hardiman issued the decision, pausing enforcement of a lower court ruling.

The panel includes appointees of President Trump, former President George W. Bush, and former President Joe Biden. Khalil is challenging Trump administration actions in his case, though the specific nature of his legal claims was not detailed in available information.
